slots.text: There was once a man who had heard, as a child, that beautiful story of how God tempted Abraham, and how Abraham stood firm in the temptation, kept the faith, and, against all expectation, received a son a second time. As he grew older, he read that same story with even greater admiration; for life had separated what had been united in the child’s pious simplicity. The older he grew, the more often his thoughts turned to that story. His enthusiasm grew stronger and stronger, and yet he could understand the story less and less. At last he forgot everything else over it. His soul had only one wish — to see Abraham — and only one longing: to have been a witness to that event. What he craved was not to see the fair lands of the East, nor the earthly splendor of the land of promise, nor that God-fearing married couple whose old age God blessed, nor the patriarch’s venerable figure, full of years, nor the blooming youth of Isaac, the gift of God — he would not have minded if the same thing had taken place on a barren heath. What he yearned for was to go along on the three-day journey on which Abraham rode with sorrow before him and Isaac at his side. His wish was to be there in the hour when Abraham raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah far off, the hour when he left the donkeys behind and went up the mountain alone with Isaac; for what absorbed him was not the imagination’s artful weaving but the shudder of thought.

That man was not a thinker. He felt no need to get beyond faith. To him it seemed that it must be the most glorious thing of all to be remembered as its father, and an enviable lot to possess it, even if no one knew.
That man was not a learned exegete; he did not know Hebrew. Had he known Hebrew, perhaps he would easily have understood the story of Abraham.
“And God tempted Abraham, and said to him: Take Isaac, your only son, the one you love, and go into the land of Moriah, and there sacrifice him as a burnt offering on a mountain I will show you.”

It was early morning. Abraham rose early, had the donkeys saddled and left his tent, taking Isaac with him; but from the window Sarah followed them with her eyes, down through the valley, until she could no longer see them. For three days they rode in silence. On the morning of the fourth day Abraham said not a single word, but raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah far off. He left the young servants behind and, with Isaac by the hand, went up the mountain alone. But Abraham said to himself: “At any rate I will not hide from Isaac where this road is leading him.” He stopped and laid his hand on Isaac’s head to bless him, and Isaac bent down to receive the blessing. And Abraham’s face was fatherliness itself, his look gentle, his speech full of exhortation. But Isaac could not understand him; his soul could not be lifted up. He threw his arms around Abraham’s knees, he fell pleading at his feet, he begged for his young life, for his bright hopes; he reminded him of the joy in Abraham’s house, he reminded him of the sorrow and the loneliness. Then Abraham raised the boy up and led him along by the hand, speaking words of comfort and exhortation. But Isaac could not understand him. Abraham climbed Mount Moriah, but Isaac did not understand him. Then for a moment Abraham turned away from him; but when Isaac looked at Abraham’s face a second time, it had changed. His look was wild, his figure was horror. He gripped Isaac by the chest, flung him to the ground and said: “Stupid boy, do you believe I am your father? I am an idol-worshipper. Do you believe it is God’s command? No, it is my own desire.” Then Isaac trembled and in his anxiety cried out: “God in heaven, have mercy on me! God of Abraham, have mercy on me! If I have no father on earth, be my father yourself!” But Abraham whispered to himself: “Lord in heaven, I thank you. After all, it is better that he believes I am a monster than that he loses his faith in you.”

When it is time to wean the child, the mother blackens her breast; it would surely be a shame for the breast to look so inviting when the child must not have it. Then the child believes the breast has changed; but the mother, she is the same, and her look is as loving and tender as ever. Happy the one who needed no more terrible means to wean the child!

It was early morning. Abraham rose early and embraced Sarah, the bride of his old age, and she kissed Isaac, her pride, her hope through all generations, who had taken away her shame. Then they rode in silence along the road, and Abraham’s eyes were fixed on the ground until the fourth day, when he raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah a long way off, but his eyes turned again to the ground. Without a word he arranged the wood and bound Isaac; without a word he drew the knife. Then he caught sight of the ram that God had chosen. That he sacrificed, and went home. — — — From that day on, Abraham aged; he could not forget that God had demanded it of him. Isaac flourished as before; but Abraham’s eye was darkened, and he saw joy no more.

When the child has grown big and it is time to wean it, the mother hides her bosom with a maiden’s modesty, and so the child no longer has a mother. Happy the child who did not lose its mother in any other way!

It was early morning. Abraham rose early and kissed Sarah, the young mother, and she kissed Isaac, her delight, her joy for all time. And Abraham rode along the road, lost in thought; he was thinking of Hagar and the son, whom he had driven out into the desert. He climbed Mount Moriah; he drew the knife.

It was a still evening. Abraham rode out alone, and he rode to Mount Moriah; he fell on his face and begged God to forgive him his sin — that he had wanted to sacrifice Isaac, that the father had forgotten his duty to the son. Many more times he rode that lonely road, but he could find no rest. To him it was incomprehensible that it should be a sin to have wanted to sacrifice to God the best thing he owned — the thing for which he would gladly have given his own life many times over. And if it was a sin — if, that is, he had not loved Isaac in that way — then he could not understand that it could be forgiven; for what sin was more terrible?

When it is time to wean the child, the mother is not without sorrow either: sorrow that she and the child are separated more and more, that the child who first lay beneath her heart, and afterwards still rested at her breast, is no longer to be so near. So together they grieve the brief grief. Happy the one who kept the child so near, and did not need to grieve any more!

It was early morning. In Abraham’s house everything had been made ready for the journey. He took his leave of Sarah; the faithful servant Eliezer went with him a stretch of the way and then turned back. Abraham and Isaac rode on together in harmony until they reached Mount Moriah. But Abraham prepared everything for the sacrifice, calm and gentle; yet as he turned away and drew the knife, Isaac saw Abraham’s left hand clench in despair and a trembling pass through his body — but Abraham drew the knife.

Then they came home again. Sarah hurried out to meet them, but Isaac had lost his faith. Nothing has ever been said of it in the world; Isaac never spoke to a living soul about what he had seen, and Abraham had no inkling that anyone had seen it.
When it is time to wean the child, the mother has the stronger food ready, so that the child shall not perish. Happy the one who has the stronger food ready.

In this way, and in many similar ways, the man of whom we are speaking thought about this event. And every time he came home after a journey to Mount Moriah, he sank down with weariness, folded his hands and said: “Still, there was no one as great as Abraham; who is capable of understanding him?”
